text:
Chinese-owned mining company Congo Dongfang International Mining (CDM) must pay $6 million in compensation to three communities affected by an industrial wastewater spill in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo), despite having suspended its operations, the country's mines ministry said on Friday.
Abandoned mine in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Credit: Courtesy of PAX Chinese mining company CDM has been ordered to pay $6 million in compensation to three Congolese communities following a toxic wastewater spill in Lubumbashi. The spill, which occurred in November 2025, released lead, arsenic, and other harmful substances into local waterways, causing biodiversity loss and health concerns. Despite suspending operations, CDM must still fulfil its compensation obligations, with delays attributed to the company's cited financial difficulties. The case highlights mounting legal and environmental pressure as more Congolese residents pursue damages for pollution by major mining operators. CDM is a major player in Congo's copper and cobalt industry , supplying battery materials to the global electric vehicle sector.
The incident occurred after wastewater escaped from a containment basin at the company's facility in Lubumbashi, the country's second-largest city, which has a population of more than 3 million.
An investigation commissioned by the government found high concentrations of lead, arsenic, and other toxic substances in the water, alongside evidence of biodiversity loss. The basin was originally designed to retain water but was reportedly being used to store acidic solutions, Reuters reported.
DR Congo's Mines Minister Louis Watum had previously criticised the company's waste management infrastructure, saying its storage and processing facilities did not meet international standards.
Authorities suspended CDM's operations for three months following the incident. However, the mines ministry said the company remained obligated to fulfil its compensation commitments even after recently announcing another suspension of activities.
The ministry attributed delays in implementing the compensation programme partly to financial difficulties cited by CDM. The company is also required to pay a separate $6.6 million penalty into the state treasury.
The compensation dispute adds to growing legal and environmental pressure on mining companies operating in the country.
Twenty-seven residents living near a Chinese-controlled copper and cobalt mine are seeking $6.3 million in damages over alleged pollution and potential health risks. The claimants, including eight children, are demanding $1.3 million for alleged personal harm and $5 million for environmental restoration.
Earlier cases have also targeted mining operators. In 2014, a court in Kipushi ordered Compagnie Minière du Sud Katanga (CMSK), Gecamines, and the Congolese government to pay $6,000 to victims who accused mining activities of contaminating the Kafubu River and destroying farmland and fish ponds.
In May 2023, residents of Kalongo and Mulomba near Kolwezi also sued Kalongwe Mining over alleged sulphuric acid discharges and toxic waste contamination of local waterways.
As the world's largest cobalt producer and second-largest copper producer, DR Congo has increasingly tightened mining regulations to strengthen oversight and protect state revenues.
